In this study, oriented samples were collected from places where the time - temperature - fluid histories had been previ- ously documented from isotopic, chemical, and petrographic studies. The magnetizations were first measured, and then the oxygen isotopic compositions of the hematite and coeval clay minerals in the same samples were determined and used to characterize the temperature, isotopic composition, and origin of the fluids from which the hematite was deposited. In this way, relationships between observed magnetizations and iso- topically characterized fluid events could be established. Thus, it appears that A, B, and possibly also C magnetizations are present across the entire basin. The drill-core data of Fahrig et al. (1978) also indicate that within a single drill hole, zones of A, B, and occasionally C magnetizations occur. Because their results contained both positive and negative inclinations, Fahrig et al. (1978) interpreted them as evidence for geomagnetic reversals during initial deposition of the sedi- ments. However, the hematite within the Athabasca Basin is diagenetic and possesses a CRM that was formed long after sedimentation. Moreover, the mean inclinations are not accurately opposed as would be expected from sequential reversals. Therefore, the positive and negative inclinations are not evidence of sequential reversals recorded during sedimen- tation but instead map the migration paths of temporally dis- tinct diagenetic fluids. A magnetizations occur in sandstone from the base of the Manitou Falls Formation and paleoregolith near the uncon- formity at the Key Lake mine site but are absent near to the fault zones that contain only the B magnetizations (Fig. 10a). In this study, oriented samples were collected from places where the time - temperature - fluid histories had been previ- ously documented from isotopic, chemical, and petrographic studies. They contain seven major dyke swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. C., Canada V8L 3x9 Received November 5th, 199 1 Revision accepted April 9th, 1992 The Queen Charlotte Islands form the western margin of the Tertiary Queen Charlotte Basin, which is situated on the western margin of the North American Plate. They contain seven major dyke swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. They contain seven major dyke swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. They contain seven major dyke swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. They contain seven major dyke swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. swarms of Late Eocene to Miocene age, a period when the relative motions of the Pacific and the North American plates in this region were dominantly dextral strike slip (transform margin), with intervals of highly oblique divergence and convergence. Within each swarm, dykes have a systematic trend. However, trends vary from swarm to swarm, indicating that the stress field varied. A total of 678 cores (1352 speci- mens) were collected from 129 dykes in six swarms over a distance of about 200 km. Magnetic stability is variable. One hundred and one dykes yielded records of the paleofield. Data are also reported from an Oligocene pluton (5 sites, 27 cores, 52 specimens) and Miocene lavas (8 sites, 52 cores, 101 specimens). Both normal and reversed magnetizations occur, but irrespective of sign, the mean directions of remanent magnetization of each swarm and of the pluton and the lavas have syste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect t

yste- matically steeper inclinations than the value calculated from coeval rocks in North America. To explain this it is proposed that, after dyke emplacement, the sampling areas were tilted to the north or northwest by amounts that vary between 9 and 16". Apparently, crustal tilting, similar in magnitude and direction, extended over distances of approximately 200 km. This cannot reflect tilting of a single block. Instead, it is argued that at least the southern Queen Charlotte Islands underwent considerable northerly or north-northwesterly directed extension and normal block faulting, which followed and in part was concurrent with the formation of widespread mid-Tertiary dyke swarms, plutons and lava flows. Making use of the fact that dykes propagate perpendicular to the direction of extension, and combining previously measured dyke orientations with paleomag- netic data, three stages of extension are proposed: east - west extension sometime during the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene; north -south extension sometime in the interval Late Oligocene to Early Miocene; and northwest-southeast extension some- time during Late Miocene or later time. Discussion Before we can consider the possible tectonic significance, of our results the age and origin of the magnetizations must be discussed. The Alto Palena Fm. and North Patagonian batholith sites all have normal polarity. Because a considerable thickness of APF was sampled, and because acquisition of TRM by the slow-cooling NPB presumably took a long time, it seems fairly certain that all our sites acquired their magneti- zation during a time when the geomagnetic field remained normal for a long time. However, the existence of sporadic outcrops of mylonitic and cataclastic rocks with N-S subhorizontal lin- eations parallel to the LOFZ is evidence that lateral motion has occurred. PALEOMAGNETISM OF LOWER CRETACEOUS ROCKS 541 In the present study we have continued to search for rotations and displacements associated with the LOFZ. Initially we planned to sample rocks of early Cretaceous age thought to be pre- sent on both sides of the fault zone. However, as the study progressed it became clear that the age of the "early Cretaceous" rocks west of the LOFZ is very poorly constrained, and that the rocks themselves tend to be poor recorders of the an- cient geomagnetic field. Therefore, in this paper we shall present only results from east of the fault. 2. Regional geological setting In contrast to the central Andes, where episodic eastward migration of the magmatic arc and a well-developed forearc fold and thrust belt are present, the Andean Cordillera between 41°S and 49°S shows a uni

r trench-parallel strike-slip faults [20-22]. We speculate that the LOFZ has accommodated shear arising from oblique subduction of the Nazca plate, and also has partly controlled the location of the Cenozoic magmatic arc. In the region between 42°S and 44°S three distinct lithologic belts parallel the LOFZ (Fig. 1). These are, from west to east, the Coastal Range Paleozoic forearc accretionary complex [23,24], the North Patagonian batholith, and a sequence of Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous vol- canic and volcanogenic sedimentary rocks. The accretionary complex consists of low-grade metasedimentary rocks and interbedded tholeitic basalts. In the east these are intruded by the North Patagonian batholith (NPB), giving rise to isolated exposures of medium to high-grade metamorphic rocks. The NPB is composed of several distinct belts that grade eastward from mostly Mio-Pliocene granodiorites and tonalites to Jurassic-Lower Cretaceous monzogranites [16]. The western margin of the NPB is cut by the main trace of the LOFZ, along which younger intrusive bodies have been emplaced syntectoni- cally. PALEOMAGNETISM OF LOWER CRETACEOUS ROCKS 541 In the present study we have continued to search for rotations and displacements associated with the LOFZ. Initially we planned to sample rocks of early Cretaceous age thought to be pre- sent on both sides of the fault zone. However, as the study progressed it became clear that the age of the "early Cretaceous" rocks west of the LOFZ is very poorly constrained, and that the rocks themselves tend to be poor recorders of the an- cient geomagnetic field. Therefore, in this paper we shall present only results from east of the fault. 2. Regional geological setting In contrast to the central Andes, where episodic eastward migration of the magmatic arc and a well-developed forearc fold and thrust belt are present, the Andean Cordillera between 41°S and 49°S shows a uni

r trench-parallel strike-slip faults [20-22]. We speculate that the LOFZ has accommodated shear arising from oblique subduction of the Nazca plate, and also has partly controlled the location of the Cenozoic magmatic arc. In the region between 42°S and 44°S three distinct lithologic belts parallel the LOFZ (Fig. 1). These are, from west to east, the Coastal Range Paleozoic forearc accretionary complex [23,24], the North Patagonian batholith, and a sequence of Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous vol- canic and volcanogenic sedimentary rocks. The accretionary complex consists of low-grade metasedimentary rocks and interbedded tholeitic basalts. In the east these are intruded by the North Patagonian batholith (NPB), giving rise to isolated exposures of medium to high-grade metamorphic rocks. The NPB is composed of several distinct belts that grade eastward from mostly Mio-Pliocene granodiorites and tonalites to Jurassic-Lower Cretaceous monzogranites [16]. The western margin of the NPB is cut by the main trace of the LOFZ, along which younger intrusive bodies have been emplaced syntectoni- cally. These sedimentary cycles are clearly related to the precessional cycle of the Earth's orbit [16]. Although the weathering profile shows quite sharp changes in colour and induration, the changes in fresh, unweathered sediment are much more gradual. Considerable effort was taken to remove the weathered surface (up to 1 m) in order to expose the fresh (dark grey, light and dark blue) sediment. This method proved suc- cessful for almost the entire intervals sampled, except for the top part of the upper Thvcra interval where the uppermost white layer re- mained visibly and strongly weathered. In the lower Thvera interval the colour layering was not as clear as in the higher part of the section. Only a greyish and a beige layer could be distin- guished, while between these two layers there was a somewhat lighter coloured (white?) layer. Sampling was carried out by taking oriented cores, 25 mm in diameter, more or less parallel to the bedding plane at very close intervals (~ 1 cm), from a freshly cut, near-vertical plane. Introduction During most of the Cenozoic, South America drifted as an isolated continent carrying a unique biota. This isolation and faunal endemism changed after the formation of the Isthmus of Panama and the corresponding influx of immi- grant taxa from North America during the late Cenozoic, resulting in what has been termed the "Great American Interchange" [1,2]. This inter- change occurred in several phases, beginning in the late Miocene, about 8-9 myr ago, but the major phase of mammalian dispersal occurred during the Pliocene and Pleistocene, during the Uquian, Ensenadan, and Lujanian land mammal ages. These biochrons are relatively well cali- brated at certain classic localities [3-8], however, in contrast, precise age determinations of pre-in- Correspondence to: B.J. MacFadden, Florida Museum

major phase of mammalian dispersal occurred during the Pliocene and Pleistocene, during the Uquian, Ensenadan, and Lujanian land mammal ages. These biochrons are relatively well cali- brated at certain classic localities [3-8], however, in contrast, precise age determinations of pre-in- Correspondence to: B.J. MacFadden, Florida Museum of Natural History, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32611, USA. terchange faunas and mammal ages in South America are relatively infrequent. The basin deposits of the central Andes of Bolivia preserve a rich sequence of mammalian faunal evolution for much of the Cenozoic. Hav- ing been deposited in a tectonically active setting, these basins often contain long, continuous strati- graphic sections of the kind amenable to magne- tostratigraphic analyses. Over the past few years, we have studied and sampled the late Cenozoic sediments surrounding the village of Inchasi in eastern Bolivia. Our collections have revealed a relatively rare pre-interchange mammalian fauna. These discoveries, in conjunction with new mag- netostratigraphic data presented for the Inchasi beds, allow a better understanding of the en- demic mammals and precise calibration of the Pliocene of the central Andes. It is perhaps significant that results reported to be of Devonian age from two rock units in the USSR (Table 1) resemble Devonian results from Britain. They are, however, of limited reliability and should be interpreted with caution. It is timely that a re-evaluation of palaeomagnetic data from the Russian plate (including the Russian platform) be made, enabling proper comparison of Russian and British data. We have already intimated that this would leave a large Mid-Palaeozoic gap in the APW record for the Russian plate. Therefore new field work and palaeomag- netic analysis have been carried out on Siluro-Devonian rocks of the Russian platform in an attempt to unveil demonstrably primary remanent magnetizations and so fill in the gap in APW. This paper offers a detailed description of those new data and of their implications for the timing of assembly of the ‘Old Red Continent’. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: MARY Comparison of published palaeomagnetic data from the Russian platform and Britain for Mid-Palaeozoic times places an ocean between the two of the order of 2000 km latitudinal width. This contradicts geological evidence, which favours contiguity between the two continental units by Devonian times. We propose that this discrepancy can be attributed to the incorrect dating of palaeomagnetic remanence. We strove to remedy this situation by conducting a new palaeomagnetic investigation of Silurian and Devonian sediments in west Ukraine, USSR (latitude 48.7"N, longitude 26"E). That investigation uncovered a pervasive Upper Palaeozoic remagnetization corresponding to a palaeomagnetic pole at lat. 45.8"S, long. 348.2"E, dpldm 1.6"/3.1", N = 25 sites (reversed polarity). A second primary or near-primary Devonian remanence was identified with pole at lat. 3.7"N, long. 325.5"E, dpldm 5.2"/8.7", N = 25 samples (mixed polarity). The age determination for this Devonian result is based on its dual polarity, evidence for a detrital remanent mode, and early host mineral phase (haematite). The new Devonian result for the Russian platform is conformable with the Devonian parts of the British apparent polar wander paths and therefore eliminates the aforementioned dis- crepancy between palaeomagnetic and geological evidence for the timing of assembly of the 'Old Red Continent'. It is perhaps significant that results reported to be of Devonian age from two rock units in the USSR (Table 1) resemble Devonian results from Britain. They are, however, of limited reliability and should be interpreted with caution. It is timely that a re-evaluation of palaeomagnetic data from the Russian plate (including the Russian platform) be made, enabling proper comparison of Russian and British data. We have already intimated that this would leave a large Mid-Palaeozoic gap in the APW record for the Russian plate. Therefore new field work and palaeomag- netic analysis have been carried out on Siluro-Devonian rocks of the Russian platform in an attempt to unveil demonstrably primary remanent magnetizations and so fill in the gap in APW. THE CHOICE OF PALAEOMAGNETIC SAMPLING REGION Silurian limestones and Devonian red sand and siltstones outcropping along the Dniester River in Podolia, west Ukraine (Fig. 4), were selected as promising rocks for palaeomagnetic analysis; with the specific intention of resolving the aforementioned palaeomagnetic discrepancy. The previous palaeomagnetic analyses of these rocks had indicated multicomponent natural remanent magnetization (NRM) but had furnished few constraints on the direction of an elusive high-stability remanence component. Moreover, those rocks are (1) well-dated biostratigraphically, (2) of an appropriate age. (3) varied in lithology, and (4) accessible. eld mapping in Honduras faces four main difficulties: poor accessibility, limited outcrop areas, lack of marker beds, and scarcity of diagnostic fossils. Because of logistical problems, only the central part of the republic has been mapped in some detail, and our interpretations pertain only to this area. In this subtropical environment, fresh outcrops are largely restricted to river beds and usually are of limited stratigraphic extent. The paucity of good outcrops combined with the lack of marker bed makes it often impossible to correlate between isolated outcrops. The direction of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of rock samples can, under certain conditions, be used for stratigraphic correlations. Most mag- netostratigraphic studies, such as the correlation of sedimentary cores from the ocean basins (e.g Kennett 1980) or the exact definition of the Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary (e.g. Alvarez et al. 1982), are based on the occurrence of reversals of the geomagnetic field and their correlation with the sea-floor magnetic anomaly time-scale. eld mapping in Honduras faces four main difficulties: poor accessibility, limited outcrop areas, lack of marker beds, and scarcity of diagnostic fossils. Because of logistical problems, only the central part of the republic has been mapped in some detail, and our interpretations pertain only to this area. In this subtropical environment, fresh outcrops are largely restricted to river beds and usually are of limited stratigraphic extent. The paucity of good outcrops combined with the lack of marker bed makes it often impossible to correlate between isolated outcrops. The direction of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of rock samples can, under certain conditions, be used for stratigraphic correlations. Most mag- netostratigraphic studies, such as the correlation of sedimentary cores from the ocean basins (e.g Kennett 1980) or the exact definition of the Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary (e.g. Alvarez et al. 1982), are based on the occurrence of reversals of the geomagnetic field and their correlation with the sea-floor magnetic anomaly time-scale. t lake sediments (e.g. Creer & Tucholka 1982) as well as older rocks (e.g. GrommC, McKee & Blake 1972). Another means of using palaeomagnetism for correlation is to compare the magnetic pole position of an unknown rock unit with the pole positions obtained from an established stratigraphic column. This will not only yield a relative age, but also an absolute age with an accuracy which depends on the age resolution of the known apparent polar wander path as well as the associated errors in the palaeomagnetic data (e.g. Porath 1967; Kyle, Ulrich & Gose 1987). Palaeomagnetic results from the Mesozoic section of Honduras delineate an apparent polar wander path which is well suited for this approach. Critical to our work is the fact that some of the rock units had been dated either by fossils or radiometrically. These dated units form the ‘calibration points’ for the apparent polar wander path, from which the ages and stratigraphic positions of unknown rock units can be inferred by comparison. Another means of using palaeomagnetism for correlation is to compare the magnetic pole position of an unknown rock unit with the pole positions obtained from an established stratigraphic column. This will not only yield a relative age, but also an absolute age with an accuracy which depends on the age resolution of the known apparent polar wander path as well as the associated errors in the palaeomagnetic data (e.g. Porath 1967; Kyle, Ulrich & Gose 1987). Palaeomagnetic results from the Mesozoic section of Honduras delineate an apparent polar wander path which is well suited for this approach. Critical to our work is the fact that some of the rock units had been dated either by fossils or radiometrically. These dated units form the ‘calibration points’ for the apparent polar wander path, from which the ages and stratigraphic positions of unknown rock units can be inferred by comparison. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: d petrologic studies fail, paleomagnetic methods may afford a useful tool with which to evaluate the amount of tilting or flexing [e.g., Beck, 1980; Faulds et al., 1988b; Dagley and Piper, 1989; Marquis and Irving, 1990]. Accurate determination of the magnitude of tilting (or flexing) of crystalline rocks with paleomagnetic data is contingent upon magnetic mineralogy and structural level of exposure. The survival of a well-defined pretilt characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) generally requires an assemblage of dominantly fine-grained (i.e., single and/or pseudo-single domain) low-Ti titanomagnetite of relatively high coercivity and moderate to high unblocking temperature, or hematite, the paragenesis of which can be determined. The presence of such magnetic grain assemblages does not guarantee, however, that a pretilt ChRM is preserved. The preservation of a pretilt ChRM is less likely at deeper crustal levels [Beck, 1980], as the probability of magnetization unblocking increases at elevated temperatures. A magnetization may even be unblocked below short-term unblocking temperatures if elevated temperatures are maintained for long periods of time [Pullaiah et al., 1975]. Consequently, the ChRM of crystalline rocks may commonly be a viscous partial thermoremanent magnetization (VPTRM), acquired during uplift-induced cooling, rather than a primary thermoremanent magnetization (TRM). carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: d petrologic studies fail, paleomagnetic methods may afford a useful tool with which to evaluate the amount of tilting or flexing [e.g., Beck, 1980; Faulds et al., 1988b; Dagley and Piper, 1989; Marquis and Irving, 1990]. Accurate determination of the magnitude of tilting (or flexing) of crystalline rocks with paleomagnetic data is contingent upon magnetic mineralogy and structural level of exposure. The survival of a well-defined pretilt characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) generally requires an assemblage of dominantly fine-grained (i.e., single and/or pseudo-single domain) low-Ti titanomagnetite of relatively high coercivity and moderate to high unblocking temperature, or hematite, the paragenesis of which can be determined. The presence of such magnetic grain assemblages does not guarantee, however, that a pretilt ChRM is preserved. The preservation of a pretilt ChRM is less likely at deeper crustal levels [Beck, 1980], as the probability of magnetization unblocking increases at elevated temperatures. A magnetization may even be unblocked below short-term unblocking temperatures if elevated temperatures are maintained for long periods of time [Pullaiah et al., 1975]. Consequently, the ChRM of crystalline rocks may commonly be a viscous partial thermoremanent magnetization (VPTRM), acquired during uplift-induced cooling, rather than a primary thermoremanent magnetization (TRM). METHODS AND PROCEDURES Representative pilot samples (about 25% of the total) were sub- jected to detailed stepwise thermal demagnetization. According to the results thus obtained, the optimal steps were chosen for the remaining part of the collection. Two speci- mens from a hand sample were always heated, their mutual orientation having been changed after each step. All measurements were made on a Czechoslovakian spin magnetometer (JR-4). The data were analyzed with stereonets and orthogonal diagrams. After isolation of components, mean vectors were calculated for each hand sample. These sample means, be- ing independent spot readings of the ancient geomagnetic field, were in turn used for computation of local- ity means or site means. The component observed in Group Ill samples (D= 311 °, 1=49 ° ), confirmed by some samples from Group II, is similar to that observed in the Nosib Group just to the south in Namibia. It is suggested that the mean Group Ill result gives the primary direction of the Chela Group, that the data support the correlation of the Nosib and Chela Groups and that the Chela rocks were overprinted magnetically during an event sub- sequent to their tilting. This mean direction is almost the same as the in situ directions of welded tuffs from four formations distributed around the Akiyoshi Plateau, which have been already reported by previous study. These welded tuffs have fission track ages between 85 and 94 Ma. The remagnetized direction is also rather similar to the well-known paleomagnetic direction for Southwest Japan before about 15 Ma. These correspon- dences suggest that the Akiyoshi limestone and the welded tuffs were remagnetized by some event after about 90 Ma and before 15 Ma. Results of thermal demagneti- zation and observation in thin sections of the limestone suggest that dominant magnetic particle is magnetite, and that the limestone may not have suffered high temperature(>500℃)alteration. This implies the presence of a low temperature chemical event. 1. Introduction Geotectonic units in Southwest Japan are characterized by a markedly zonal distribution. These tectonic zones generally become younger from north to south, on the basis of paleontologic evidence (OZAWA et al.,1985). It has been suspected that the zonal d

l authors proposed that such accreted terranes had been originally formed at a much lower latitude than their present positions, on the basis of paleomagnetic investigations of sedimentary and volcanic rocks distributed in the terranes (HATTORI and HIR00KA, 1979; TAIRA, 89 90 H. MORINAGA et al. 1981; HATTORI, 1982; HIROOKA et al., 1983; SHIBUYA et al., 1983; SHIBUYA and SASAJIMA, 1986). Because the terranes in Japan have repeatedly suffered severe tectonic move- ments, rocks in the terranes must have been located under an environment where they probably tended to acquire secondary magnetization. Based on detailed progressive thermal demagnetization treatments, SHIBUYA and SASAJIMA (1986) reported that red cherts and red siliceous mudstones from the Inuyama area in the southern part of the Mino terrane contain very stable secondary components. Radiolarian age determination (YAO et al.,1980) suggests the middle Triassic to the middle Jurassic age for these rocks. The Mino terrane was emplaced through accretion during the Jurassic (TAIRA et al., 1981). Conclusion The main finding of this study is that the Aulis volcanics in the Lesser Himalaya possess a highly complex multi-component remanent magnetization. The rocks have experienced at least three magnetization/ remagnetization episodes besides the recent magnetization. These magnetic components seem to rest on distinct mineralogical phases produced chemically from the original titanomagnetite contain- ed in the rocks during initial cooling. These components can be resolved by an integrated cleaning approach such as AF-followed-TH demagnetization . The Aulis Volcanics, though of limited distribution, seem to be representative rocks for understanding the magnetomineralogical consequences of low-temperature oxidation. These rocks also show that the process of alteration and its magnetic consequence vary in accordance with the micro-environmental conditions , which in turn are time-dependent (STORETVEDT,1973). 116 P. Conclusion The main finding of this study is that the Aulis volcanics in the Lesser Himalaya possess a highly complex multi-component remanent magnetization. The rocks have experienced at least three magnetization/ remagnetization episodes besides the recent magnetization. These magnetic components seem to rest on distinct mineralogical phases produced chemically from the original titanomagnetite contain- ed in the rocks during initial cooling. These components can be resolved by an integrated cleaning approach such as AF-followed-TH demagnetization . The Aulis Volcanics, though of limited distribution, seem to be representative rocks for understanding the magnetomineralogical consequences of low-temperature oxidation. These rocks also show that the process of alteration and its magnetic consequence vary in accordance with the micro-environmental conditions , which in turn are time-dependent (STORETVEDT,1973). 116 P. Conclusion The main finding of this study is that the Aulis volcanics in the Lesser Himalaya possess a highly complex multi-component remanent magnetization. The rocks have experienced at least three magnetization/ remagnetization episodes besides the recent magnetization. These magnetic components seem to rest on distinct mineralogical phases produced chemically from the original titanomagnetite contain- ed in the rocks during initial cooling. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: (Received November 10,1987; Revised August 25, 1988) Detailed paleomagnetic investigation was carried out on 33 trachyte and trachyandesite rock samples collected at 5 sites from the Aulis volcanics in the Tansen area, the Lesser Himalaya, Nepal. Analysis of magnetic behavior by stepwise alternating field (up to 53 mT) and then thermal demagnetization shows complex multi-component remanence composed of at least four components as follows:1)Component A(D=001°,I=47°)-of recent field origin,2)Component B (D=339°,I=32°)-interpreted as acquired during early Miocene,3)Component C (D=330°,I=-49°)-probably acquired during Late Cretaceous, and 4)Component D,poorly defined, with southerly declination and downward inclination of about 55°-probably acquired prior the acquisition of component C. All these compo- nents show in situ grouping suggesting their secondary nature. Thermomagnetic analysis showed double-Curie point curves indicating two major magnetic phases with Curie temperatures around 565℃ and 360℃. These phases are interpreted as of Ti-poor magnetite and titanomaghemite, respectively, which were formed due to low-temperature oxidation of original titanomaenetite. Analysis of unblocking temperature spectra suggests that the 360℃phase contri- butes to the component B magnetization. 1. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: tions of very high pH and low pE (HENSHAW and MERRILL, 1980). It takes some 500 years of deposition for pyritization to take place (MANNING et al., 1979). Unless the sediments contain a source of hydrogen sulfide, the iron hydroxides and oxide are likely to be oxidized to hematite, which takes a few million years. Metamorphism is the other factor in the production of magnetic minerals. When rocks bearing, Fe, Ti02 and S2 are heated, pyrrhotite or hematite can be formed (MIYASHIR0, 1965). The alternative production of pyrrhotite or hematite is controlled by the O2 and S2 fugacities (ITAYA et al., 1985). Pyrrhotite never coexists with hematite, whereas magnetite can coexist with hematite. Metamorphism can produce a sedimentary layer which bears either hematite or pyrrhotite. The two hypotheses were examined through microscopic observation. Micro- Remagnetization of Cambrian to Triassic Sedimentary Rocks133 scopic study indicates that hematite-bearing slate and quartzite contain much authigenic magnesian and ferric minerals. They are composed of chlorite, white mica, and biotite. Authigenic fine magnesian and ferric minerals are also observed in the pyrrhotite-bearing Tumudong limestone. These facts strongly indicate that the sedimentary layers in the Paegunsan Syncline were more or less metamorphosed. This study evaluates the deformation associated with the collision of the Izu block with Honshu. About 900 volcanic rock samples ranging in age from 0.2 to 1.5 Ma were measured. A mean paleomagnetic direction(D=3.5° I=64.4° α95=5.10) of the Chichibu Quartz Diorite, obtained from 21 samples, shows no significantly deflected declination. This indicates no tectonic rotation of the Kanto Mountains since intrusion of the Chichibu Quartz Diorite (6-8 Ma). This result signifies that the cusp in the pre-Neogene zonal structure (Kanto Syntaxis) was formed in the Late Miocene or earlier. 1. Further, HYODO and NIITSUMA (1986) referred mean paleomagnetic directions of the Chichibu Tertiary System to clockwise rotation of the Kanto Mountains at about 94°since the Early Miocene. They explained this rotation by the opening of the Japan Sea(45°,15 Ma;OTOFUJI et al.,1985)and by the collision of the Tanzawa Block(45°, after 6-7 Ma;NIITSUMA,1982). On the other hand, ITOH (1988) carried out a paleomagnetic study on Late Cretaceous and Miocene rocks in the eastern part of Southwest Japan, and concluded that the bending motion occurred between 15 and 12 Ma. Thus several timings have been considered for the cusp formation. The Kanto Mountains are on the east wing of the cusp, and the Chichibu Quartz Diorite intrudes into the central part of the Kanto Mountains (Fig. 2). The radiometric ages of this quartz diorite determined by UENO and SHIBATA (1986) all indicate the Late Miocene (6-8 Ma). We measured paleomagnetism of the Chichibu Quartz Diorite and concluded that the cusp in the zonal structure had been formed in the Late Miocene or earlier. 2. Paleomagnetic Measurements Remanent magnetization was measured by an ScT C-113 cryogenic magneto- meter and a Natsuhara-Liken SMM-86 spinner magnetometer. To investigate the stability of the remanence, three to four specimens were selected from each site and subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization. Specimens were heated in air. We also conducted stepwise alternating field demagnetization to test the stability of the remanence. However, the apparatus used could produce a maximum field of only 25 mT; in many cases, the field was too weak to remove secondary components sufficiently. The thermal demagnetization is, however, generally more successful in removing overprints than the alternating field method (e.g., ITOH,1988). Therefore, only the results of the thermal demagnetization are described and discussed in this paper. Two types of behavior on progressive thermal demagnetization were commonly observed on vector demagnetization diagrams. The first type (Type A) shows the stable nature of the remanence (Fig. 4). Introduction In recent years, many paleomagnetic studies have been conducted regarding the time and manner of deformation of the Japan Arc at the time of the opening of the Japan Sea. OTOFUJI and MATSUDA (1983) showed that Southwest Japan (west of the Itoigawa-Shizuoka Tectonic Line) rotated clockwise with the opening of the Japan Sea between 28 Ma and 12 Ma. OTOFUJI et al. Geological Setting and Sampling The Miocene Matsushimawan Group is exposed in the area around Matsushima Bay, Northeast Japan. It unconformably overlies bedrocks of pre-Tertiary age, and is unconformably covered by the Shida Group of the middle to late Miocene. The stratigraphy of the Matsushimawan Group is summarized in Fig. 2 (ISHII et al., 1982, 1983a). It is divided into five lithostratigraphic units: the Shiogama, Sauramachi, Ajiri, Matsushima and Otsuka Formations, in ascending order. Introduction The Japan Sea-Japanese island-arcs is one of back-arc basin-island-arc systems on the eastern margin of Eurasia. The ages and opening histories of back-arc basins have been ordinarily revealed by means of identifications of magnetic anomaly stripes in the basins (e.g., WEISSEL, 1981). Howe

rcs implies the initiation of the Japan Sea opening prior to the opening accompanied with the CW rotation of the Southwest Japan block at about 15 Ma (KANO and YANAGISAWA, 1989). Hence, it is indispensable to clarify the drifting mode of Southwest Japan in more detail, especially the extent of the CW-rotated block and the preferable position of the rotation pivot, for the better understanding of the whole process of the opening of the Japan Sea. The Tsushima Strait area between the Korean Peninsula and Kyushu Island is regarded as a boundary region between the stable Asian continent and the CW-rotated Southwest Japan block during the formation of the Japan Sea (Fig, 1). Miocene tectonics in the area must have been controlled by a relative motion between the two blocks. Seismic reflection profiles in the Tsushima Strait area show the existence of similar deformation features in the sea area (KATSURA and NAGANO, 1976; SAKURAI and NAGANO, 1976; NAGANO et al., 1976); the sediments in the area are acoustically divided into five stratigraphic layers, and the lowest layer is correlated to the Taishu Group or Goto Group on the profiles. The deformation features are recognized in the lowest layer between the two archipelagoes. SHIMADA (1977) suggested that fold and fault systems of the Taishu Group was formed due to a horizontal compressive force in NW-SE direction. On the basis of the similarity of deformation features of the pre-middle Miocene sediments, it is suggested that the Tsushima Strait area was subjected to compressive deformation after the deposition of pre-middle Miocene sediments. Since Miocene igneous rocks unconformably overlie and/or intrude the deformation features of the sediments on the two archipelagoes, the FT ages of the igneous rocks determined in this study constrain the timing of the compressive deformation to be at sometime in the early to middle Miocene before about 15 Ma. Seismic reflection profiles in the Tsushima Strait area show the existence of similar deformation features in the sea area (KATSURA and NAGANO, 1976; SAKURAI and NAGANO, 1976; NAGANO et al., 1976); the sediments in the area are acoustically divided into five stratigraphic layers, and the lowest layer is correlated to the Taishu Group or Goto Group on the profiles. The deformation features are recognized in the lowest layer between the two archipelagoes. SHIMADA (1977) suggested that fold and fault systems of the Taishu Group was formed due to a horizontal compressive force in NW-SE direction. On the basis of the similarity of deformation features of the pre-middle Miocene sediments, it is suggested that the Tsushima Strait area was subjected to compressive deformation after the deposition of pre-middle Miocene sediments. Since Miocene igneous rocks unconformably overlie and/or intrude the deformation features of the sediments on the two archipelagoes, the FT ages of the igneous rocks determined in this study constrain the timing of the compressive deformation to be at sometime in the early to middle Miocene before about 15 Ma. Untilted directions of primary magnetic components from early to middle Miocene sedimentary rocks in the Goto Islands dominantly showed counter-clockwise (CCW) deflections to the expected direction of the geocentric axial dipole field, while paleomagnetic directions from Miocene igneous rocks and Quaternary basalts were concordant with the expected direction. Zircon FT ages determined on sixteen Miocene igneous rocks show good agreement at about 15 Ma. These results, in conjunction with previously-reported paleomagnetic data in the Tsushima Islands, suggest that the Goto Islands were rotated at the early to middle Miocene before about 15 Ma and that the CCW of the Tsushima islands occurred after about 15 Ma. The CCW rotations of these islands imply that the Tsushima Strait area did not belong to the Southwest Japan block in terms of clock-wise (CW) rotation at about 15 Ma, constraining the western margin of the CW-rotated block. These results, in conjunction with previously-reported paleomagnetic data in the Tsushima Islands, suggest that the Goto Islands were rotated at the early to middle Miocene before about 15 Ma and that the CCW of the Tsushima islands occurred after about 15 Ma. The CCW rotations of these islands imply that the Tsushima Strait area did not belong to the Southwest Japan block in terms of clock-wise (CW) rotation at about 15 Ma, constraining the western margin of the CW-rotated block. The FT ages confine the time of the compressive deformation of pre-middle Miocene sediments in the area to be at the early to middle Miocene before about 15 Ma. The CCW rotations of these islands probably took place in response to the movement of the fault system in the area associated with the compressive regime, especially a sinistral motion of the Tsushima-Goto tectonic line. The early to middle Miocene compressive deformation in the area occurred almost coeval with the opening of the Japan Sea. The compressive tectonic regime implies the convergence of the western margin of the Southwest Japan block to the Korean Peninsula during the CW rotation of the block at about 15 Ma, which gives a

tectonics in the area must have been controlled by a relative motion between the two blocks. To reveal Miocene tectonics in the area will give a clue for clarifying the drifting mode of Southwest Japan, especially estimating the western extent of the block and the position of the rotation pivot. A previous paleomagnetic study on the Tsushima Islands in the area suggested that the islands were rotated counter-clockwise (CCW) by about 28‹ sometime after the middle Miocene igneous activity on the islands (ISHIKAWA et al., 1989), which implies a different tectonic regime in the Tsushima Strait area from that of Southwest Japan during the formation process of the Japan Sea. It is usually assumed that the formation of new magnetic minerals during heating will produce an observable change in magnetic susceptibility. An increase in susceptibility during thermal demagnetization is generally thought to indicate the formation of new magnetite, while a decrease in susceptibility often results from oxidation of (titano)- magnetite to (titano)hematite or inversion of (titano)maghemite to (titano)hematite (COLLINSON, 1983). Even if any of these field tests is impossible to apply, we think we can judge to some extent whether the direction should be rejected or not by the stability of NRM. We think that an NRM which shows stability to both AF and thermal demagnetizations is not of VRM origin. VRM is usually AF demagnetized in fields of 20-30 mT, known from the experiment on oceanic basalt (IRVING, 1968) and stony meteorite (NAGATA, 1981). However, a surprisingly stable VRM with high coercivities of almost 100 mT has been reported for hematitebearing sedimentary rocks (BIQUAND, 1979) and artificial samples containing fine-grained hematite (DUNLOP and STIRLING, 1977). Introduction Since the pioneering work by KAWAI et al. (1961) the island of Japan has been studied by paleomagnetism as summarized by SASAJIMA (1981). Especially after 1980, Miocene rocks have been intensively studied and the conclusion that Southwest Japan and Northeast Japan had gone through large block rotations in opposite sense, clockwise and counterclockwise respectively, with rotation angles of around 50‹ for both blocks was reached (OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983, 1987; OTOFUJI et al., 1985a, 1985b; TOSHA and HAMANO,1988). The rotations of the Japan Islands revealed by paleomagnetism are generally interpreted in relation to the opening of the Japan Sea which is a typical back-arc basin (HILDE and WAGEMAN, 1973; UYEDA and MIYASHIRO, 1974). The timing of the rotation is also well constrained by paleomagnetic data; Southwest Japan rotated within only 1 My of around

rotation angle of 20-30‹ for Northeast Japan. They even proposed that a critical review of paleomagnetism of Southwest Japan would be necessary, with emphasis on the verification of the primary origin of the NRM. Only few paleomagnetic studies have been made in Hokkaido in order to clarify its tectonic history. Paleomagnetism of Hokkaido is important not only in relation to the opening of the Japan Sea but also to clarify the collision process of East Hokkaido to the middle part of Hokkaido which is considered to have occurred as recently as after the late Miocene (KIMURA and TAMAKI, 1985). The purpose of this study is to present a paleomagnetic result from Miocene to Pliocene rocks in the Shakotan Peninsula, West Hokkaido. 2. The volcanic sequence is a continuation of the so-called Green tuff belt which covers Northeast Japan, this region is considered to be a part of Northeast Japan. nue to southeast Kyushu. We carried out a paleomagnetic study aimed at clarifying whether Tanegashima Island belongs to the Southwest Japan block and, if not, examining the possible tectonic rotation of South Kyushu, including Tanegashima Island, with respect to Eurasia or Honshu main island. 2. Geology Tanegashima Island is overlain dominantly by the Paleogene Kumage Group, which belongs to the Shimanto Supergroup in the outer zone of Southwest Japan (e.g., TAIRA et al., 1982), and the Miocene Kukinaga Group (Fig. 1). The Kumage Group, exposed in the northern and southwestern parts of this island, consists of alternating layers of sandstone and shale dipping northwestward at high angles about NNE-SSW strike. The Kumage Group is subdivided into four lithostratigraphic units; the Nijuban, Hamatsuwaki, Fukago and Sumiyoshi Formations, in ascending order (HAYASAKA et al., 1980; Fig. 2). The total thickness is more than 5000 m. Radiolarians of the Middle to Late Eocene were reported from the varicolored shales interbedded in sandstone- shale alternations of the Hamatsuwaki and Nijuban Formations (OKADA et al., 1982). nue to southeast Kyushu. We carried out a paleomagnetic study aimed at clarifying whether Tanegashima Island belongs to the Southwest Japan block and, if not, examining the possible tectonic rotation of South Kyushu, including Tanegashima Island, with respect to Eurasia or Honshu main island. 2. Geology Tanegashima Island is overlain dominantly by the Paleogene Kumage Group, which belongs to the Shimanto Supergroup in the outer zone of Southwest Japan (e.g., TAIRA et al., 1982), and the Miocene Kukinaga Group (Fig. 1). The Kumage Group, exposed in the northern and southwestern parts of this island, consists of alternating layers of sandstone and shale dipping northwestward at high angles about NNE-SSW strike. The Kumage Group is subdivided into four lithostratigraphic units; the Nijuban, Hamatsuwaki, Fukago and Sumiyoshi Formations, in ascending order (HAYASAKA et al., 1980; Fig. 2). The total thickness is more than 5000 m. Radiolarians of the Middle to Late Eocene were reported from the varicolored shales interbedded in sandstone- shale alternations of the Hamatsuwaki and Nijuban Formations (OKADA et al., 1982). Bedded sandstones of the Hamatsuwaki and Fukago Formations yielded several mollus- can fossils similar to those found in the Late Oligocene to Early Miocene Asiya

Volcanic rock samples were collected at seven and ten sites in Rarotonga and Rurutu, respectively. The mean direction of magnetization for Rarotonga is 173.8‹ in declination and 46.2‹ in inclination (k=72.0 and ƒ¿95=7.9‹) and is more reliable than that from a previous work. The mean direction for three young rock sites in Rurutu is 218.2‹ in declination and 39.5‹ in inclination (k=49.3 and ƒ¿95=17.7‹) which for five old rock sites is 188.1‹ in declination and 51.4‹ in inclination (k=254.2 and ƒ¿95= 4.8‹). These paleomagnetic results are in accordance with the total intensity anomaly pattern on each island, calculated using observed values of the geomagnetic field total intensity. The implication for the formation of these two islands inferred from the present results is consistent with that inferred from K-Ar ages and 87Sr/86Sr ratios by previous works. The formation of Rarotonga and Rurutu may be explained well by the concept of a "hot line" in a previous work rather than by the well-known "fixed hot spot" hypothesis. 1. Discussion of Results Samples from the Early Trisasic, Permian, and Middle Carboniferous formations were serverely overprinted by BNF. As many as 65% of paleomagnetic data showed only one component directions of BNF as well as random or unstable magnetizations. (1975), this would indicate that the beds acquired a thermoviscous remanence near Curie temperature in the Brunhes. The lack of any evidence of high temperature regional or contact metamorphism of the formations, however, indicates that the remagnetization process of hematite-bearing beds most likely involved the chemical precipitation or alteration of hematite, following the results of KENT and MILLER (1987) and WITTE and KENT (1991), rather than a thermoviscous resetting of existing hematite. Discussion of Results Samples from the Early Trisasic, Permian, and Middle Carboniferous formations were serverely overprinted by BNF. As many as 65% of paleomagnetic data showed only one component directions of BNF as well as random or unstable magnetizations. The maxium unblocking temperature for the BNF component in the hematite-bearing beds studied by us is in the range 600Ž to 650Ž. According to the relaxation time-blocking temperature (t-T) relations of PULLAIAH et al. (1975), this would indicate that the beds acquired a thermoviscous remanence near Curie temperature in the Brunhes. The lack of any evidence of high temperature regional or contact metamorphism of the formations, however, indicates that the remagnetization process of hematite-bearing beds most likely involved the chemical precipitation or alteration of hematite, following the results of KENT and MILLER (1987) and WITTE and KENT (1991), rather than a thermoviscous resetting of existing hematite. INTRODUCTION The study area is located in the NW part of the Himalayan range in Hazara (Pakistan) and Azad Kashmir. The large-scale tectonic structure of the region is characterized by a structural reentrant or syntaxial bend, the Hazara-Kashmir Syntaxis (HKS). Because of its complex composition and key position for the geology of the northwestern Himalayas, several very detailed stratigraphic, structural, and petrographical investigations have been undertaken on the HKS [Wadia, 1931; Calkins et al., 1975; Bossart et al., 1988; Bossart and Ottiger, 1989]. This paper presents new paleomagnetic results from three sections (Jhelum, Neelum, and Kaghan valley) across the core of the HKS. One result of previous structural investigations [Bossart et al., 1988] was the observation of increas- ing finite-strain state from south to north in the core of the syntaxis. This result was taken into consider- ation when we prepared the present study. Primary paleomagnetic directions are more likely to be found 104 Bossart et al.: Hazara-Kashmir Syntaxis, Rock Magnetic Properties, Pakistan in the southern sections than in the northern ones, where primary directions are obliterated by tectonic strain. Our paleomagnetic approach is therefore twofold. On one hand, the weakly defor

roach is therefore twofold. On one hand, the weakly deformed south- ernmost section in the Jhelum valley is useful for a regional paleogeographic and tectonic interpretation, using the primary paleomagnetic directions for determination of the paleolatitude and relative rota- tions of the Murree formation. This paleomagnetic information leads to a modification of our previous kinematic model for the formation of the syntaxis [Bossart et al., 1988], resulting in a more unique solution. On the other hand, the broad spectrum of natural strains preserved in the rocks gives informa- tion about progressive deformation. By measuring the anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS), a quali- tative agreement of the strains observed in the field and those derived from magnetic fabrics was ob- tained. Finally, a deformation path from south to north is suggested, which refers to the more local deformational aspect of the syntaxis. 2. GEOLOGICAL REVIEW 2.1. The Tectonic Structure of the Hazara-Kashmir Syntaxis The Hazara-Kashmir Syntaxis consists of a series of overlapping thrust sheets. They are made up of various Precambrian, Paleozoic, and Mesozoic formations which have been overthrust on Tertiary molasse deposits, known as the Murree formation. Two major thrusts can be distinguished: a higher Panja

tern part of the syntaxis has been displaced toward the south some tens of kilometers relative to the eastem part. Greco et al. [1989] have shown that this mylonite shear zone separates the tectonic units of the Lesser and Higher Himalaya and is therefore related to the Main Central Thrust (MCT). The core of the syntaxis (Figure 1) is best inter- preted with a dome model [Bossart et al., 1988]. The two limbs of the domal fold are characterized by a change in the bedding-cleavage relationship: in the Kaghan section, the bedding-cleavage intersection lineations (equals fold axes) dip steeply to the NE, North, and NW, whereas in the Neelum section they dip with intermediate angles to the SE (see stereo- grams of Figure 1). This domal fold in the Murree formation developed by layer compression subper- pendicular to a southwestward overthrust direction. This direction was derived by finite cleavage and stretching lineations in the Murree formation (mineral reorientation parallel to the longest axis of deformed reduction spots). The Murree thrust cuts down the Murree strata from NE to SW. The base of the Murree formation, the Muzaffarabad anticlinal structure, was refolded with SSE directed compression axes during the late de- formation phase. In particular, the dip-corrected characteristic directions of the westernmost samples (Nll-14, Figure 7B) are considerably scattered because of individual passive reorientation during refolding. Toward the east (N41-43 to N51-54) the increasing cleavage intensity starts to effect the samples. Between these two areas (N21-24 to N31- 35), where both effects are small, the directions con- form with the dip-corrected primary directions observed in the Jhelum valley (compare stereograms of Figure 7B and Figure 3, bottom fight). Hence only a very small portion of the Neelum section contains primary remanence directions. The majority of the samples have been influenced by local deformation and cannot be used for a regional tectonic interpretation. 4.2.2.AMS of Neelum section. The mylonite shear zone cuts the NW-SE directed structural trend of the syntaxis. Furthermore, it marks the transition zone of the early SW, to late SSE, transport directions. This discontinuity is the most obvious geological argument for the rotational changes of the magnetic vectors. To the north the border of rotational change is not clear. The increases in deformation and metamorphism distort the in- formation contained in the primary remanence direct- ions. The cause of the 'block rotations' to the west of the HKS might be explained by the \"salt-no salt\" model of Seeber et al., [1981]. In the syntaxis and east of it there is a strong coupling of Indian basement and cover, whereas to the southwest of it the widespread and often thick Cambrian evaporite deposits act as ideal d6collement horizons between basement and cover (Salt range). Large clockwise rotations, basement thrusting and thrusting at the surface occur simultaneously where evaporites are absent. Received 1992 December 15; in original form 1992 October 20 SUMMARY A palaeomagnetic study has been made of samples collected from Permo-Triassic type sections in the Emei Mountain region of southwest China. No results were obtained from the Lower Permian Qixia Formation limestones or the (Lower)- Upper Permian Maokou Formation limestones. The Upper Permian (Longtanian) Emeishan Basalt Formation shows excellent stability to both alternating field and thermal demagnetization. Results from 24 flows (125 samples) are all of normal polarity, have a positive fold test (Cretaceous or Tertiary folding), and give a pole position at 54.5"N, 254.3"E with dp = 1.8", dm =3.5". The basalts were thus presumably extruded after the end of the Kiaman Reversed Superchron. The overlying Upper Permian Xuanwei Formation of red mudstones and sandstones (Changxingian in age) also shows a positive fold test from N = 12 samples after thermal treatment and has a positive reversals test at level C. Here the lowest 11 flows dip at 77" towards 64" whereas the higher six flows dip at 87" towards 62" (NE). A further seven flows (36 samples) were collected in the Liujinggou section where the flows dip at 46" towards 125" (SE). The Xuanwei Formation disconformably overlies the Emeishan Basalt Formation and at the Lianghekou section consists of purplish-red claystone interbedded with purplish- grey to dark-red medium-grained sandstone with thin coal seams. Fossil floras indicate the Xuanwei Formation is latest Permian in age (Changxingian). 17 oriented samples were collected from a thickness of 40 m starting immediately above the basalts. Four samples were collected from a red mudstone band at the base of the formation just above the basalts. Here the beds dip at 87" towards 62" (NE). A further 13 samples were collected 2Sm higher in the sequence from a 15 m section of red claystones and sandstones that are slightly overturned dipping at 97" towards 57" (NE). lower half of the formation. Here the beds are again slightly overturned with dips varying from 94" to 101" through the sequence towards 65" (NE). This observation is consistent with the excellent stability to alternating field and thermal demagnetization observed in so many samples. The remaining eight samples were all of Type 3 showing a peak in susceptibility with decreasing temperature with the value finally decreasing to below its room temperature value at liquid nitrogen temperature. the Permo-Carboniferous. It is not clear by how much this event post-dates the deposition of the underlying Radium Ridge Breccias and hematitic ironstone. The latter may be Ordovician or older if earlier monazite U-Pb data are correct, and may have been formed by granite-related hydrothermal fluids. In that case, the older remanence in the breccia is also an overprint. Epithermal sinter formation and chemical (rather than purely thermal) resetting of the remanence in the underlying breccia were probably due to deep circulation of oxidized fluids during Permo-Carboniferous tectonic activity. Chemical reaction of these fluids with pre-existing magnetite-bearing ironstone may have been responsible for uranium mineralization during the Permo-Carboniferous. This interpretation is consistent with published textural, isotopic and fluid inclusion data, but an older age for the uranium concentration, as a primary part of the ironstone formation, cannot be excluded. Alternatively, if the monazite data are discarded, the entire hydrothermal process including iron, uranium and silica deposition could have occurred in the Permo-Carboniferous. Key words: hydrothermal, palaeomagnetism, sinter, uranium ore. INTRODUCTION The Mt Painter area, 550 km north of Adelaide in the northern Flinders Ranges of Sout

. The Mt Painter Inlier exposes Middle Proterozoic crystalline basement and is surrounded by Adelaidean (Late Proterozoic) sedimentary sequences. The region has experienced a complex thermal history extending through to present-day hot spring activity. The Phanerozoic thermal history of the inlier was probably influenced by the abundance of unusually uranium-rich highly fractionated alkali-feldspar granite, regarded as Palaeozoic in age (Teale 1979; Teale & Lottermoser 1987; Drexel & Major 1990). The breccia is composed dom- inantly of locally derived basement clasts which are altered and cemented to varying degrees by K-feldspar, quartz and hematite. Breccia is distributed over an area of at least 8 x 10km near the centre of the inlier (Fig. 1), and comprises forms varying from massive breccia piles to funnel-shaped bodies, with water-laid and subaerial chem- ical and mechanical sedimentary strata which are still in a near-horizontal bedding position (Youles 1975; Major 1976; Drexel & Major 1987, 1990; Higgins et al. 1988). The origin of the breccia and contained ores is debated; interpretations ranging from magmatic-hydrothermal activity associated with Ordovician (or younger) granitoid intrusion (Drexel 1980; Lambert et al. 1982), through deep hydrothermal fluid convection driven by t

-temperature supergene processes associated with deep weathering in the Tertiary (Blissett in Coats & Blissett 1971). Any information on the absolute timing of breccia formation and mineralization impacts directly on these widely disparate genetic interpretations. The typically 88 M. IDNURM AND C. A. Uraniferous breccia in the Mt Painter region The breccia deposits and associated uranium mineral- ization in the Mt Painter and Mt Gee areas have been described by Stillwell and Edwards (1954), Youles (1975, 1984, 1986), Major (1976), Drexel (1980; 1981), Lambert et al. (1982), Drexel and Major (1987, 1990) and Higgins et al. (1988). The breccia comprises a pile of variable thickness up to at least 500 m (Drexel & Major 1987), grading from in situ fractured and K-feldspar-altered basement to dominantly granitic and hematitic breccia units (the Radium Ridge Breccias) and finally to vuggy rocks consisting dominantly of quartz-hematite-rich chemical precipitates near the top (the Mt Gee Sinter; Drexel & Major 1987; Fig. 2a). The breccia is restricted to the centre of the Mt Painter basement block and there is no evidence of stratigraphic relation to the Adelaidean sequence. It shows no metamorphic recrystallization or deformation that could suggest a Delamerian regional- metamorphic overprint. No potentially coeval volcanic rocks have been identified in the region (Drexel 1980).
