Samples from the sinter were collected as blocks; and those from the other rock units as cores, the latter by means of a portable diamond drill. Sample orientations were obtained with a magnetic com- pass and, nearly always, a sun compass. The drillcores were cleaned of surface contaminants by sandblasting with fine glass grit. Strongly magnetized specimens (>200 mA/m) were measured either on a Digico spinner magnetometer or a three-axis 2G cryo- genic magnetometer. Weaker specimens were usually measured on a two-axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer. Magnetic sus- ceptibilities were measured between heatings to monitor chemical changes. Before thermal treatment, some samples were partly demagnetized in alternating fields (AF) using a Schonstedt 2-axis GSD-5 tumbler- demagnetizer. . The Mt Painter Inlier exposes Middle Proterozoic crystalline basement and is surrounded by Adelaidean (Late Proterozoic) sedimentary sequences. The region has experienced a complex thermal history extending through to present-day hot spring activity. The Phanerozoic thermal history of the inlier was probably influenced by the abundance of unusually uranium-rich highly fractionated alkali-feldspar granite, regarded as Palaeozoic in age (Teale 1979; Teale & Lottermoser 1987; Drexel & Major 1990). The breccia is composed dom- inantly of locally derived basement clasts which are altered and cemented to varying degrees by K-feldspar, quartz and hematite. Breccia is distributed over an area of at least 8 x 10km near the centre of the inlier (Fig. 1), and comprises forms varying from massive breccia piles to funnel-shaped bodies, with water-laid and subaerial chem- ical and mechanical sedimentary strata which are still in a near-horizontal bedding position (Youles 1975; Major 1976; Drexel & Major 1987, 1990; Higgins et al. 1988). The origin of the breccia and contained ores is debated; interpretations ranging from magmatic-hydrothermal activity associated with Ordovician (or younger) granitoid intrusion (Drexel 1980; Lambert et al. 1982), through deep hydrothermal fluid convection driven by t

-temperature supergene processes associated with deep weathering in the Tertiary (Blissett in Coats & Blissett 1971). Uraniferous breccia in the Mt Painter region The breccia deposits and associated uranium mineral- ization in the Mt Painter and Mt Gee areas have been described by Stillwell and Edwards (1954), Youles (1975, 1984, 1986), Major (1976), Drexel (1980; 1981), Lambert et al. (1982), Drexel and Major (1987, 1990) and Higgins et al. (1988). The breccia comprises a pile of variable thickness up to at least 500 m (Drexel & Major 1987), grading from in situ fractured and K-feldspar-altered basement to dominantly granitic and hematitic breccia units (the Radium Ridge Breccias) and finally to vuggy rocks consisting dominantly of quartz-hematite-rich chemical precipitates near the top (the Mt Gee Sinter; Drexel & Major 1987; Fig. 2a). The breccia is restricted to the centre of the Mt Painter basement block and there is no evidence of stratigraphic relation to the Adelaidean sequence. It shows no metamorphic recrystallization or deformation that could suggest a Delamerian regional- metamorphic overprint. No potentially coeval volcanic rocks have been identified in the region (Drexel 1980). Samples from the sinter were collected as blocks; and those from the other rock units as cores, the latter by means of a portable diamond drill. Sample orientations were obtained with a magnetic com- pass and, nearly always, a sun compass. The drillcores were cleaned of surface contaminants by sandblasting with fine glass grit. Strongly magnetized specimens (>200 mA/m) were measured either on a Digico spinner magnetometer or a three-axis 2G cryo- genic magnetometer. Weaker specimens were usually measured on a two-axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer. The specimens were demagnetized thermally in either a small Schonstedt TSD-1 demagnetizer or large furnaces described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Magnetic sus- ceptibilities were measured between heatings to monitor chemical changes. Before thermal treatment, some samples were partly demagnetized in alternating fields (AF) using a Schonstedt 2-axis GSD-5 tumbler- demagnetizer. The breccia comprises a pile of variable thickness up to at least 500 m (Drexel & Major 1987), grading from in situ fractured and K-feldspar-altered basement to dominantly granitic and hematitic breccia units (the Radium Ridge Breccias) and finally to vuggy rocks consisting dominantly of quartz-hematite-rich chemical precipitates near the top (the Mt Gee Sinter; Drexel & Major 1987; Fig. 2a). carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: LABORATORY TECHNIQUES For the palaeomagnetic study, more than 200 samples were collected from granitic and hematitic breccia units, sinter deposits and diamictite at eleven localities in the Mt Painter region (Fig. 1). Samples from the sinter were collected as blocks; and those from the other rock units as cores, the latter by means of a portable diamond drill. Sample orientations were obtained with a magnetic com- pass and, nearly always, a sun compass. The drillcores were cleaned of surface contaminants by sandblasting with fine glass grit. Strongly magnetized specimens (>200 mA/m) were measured either on a Digico spinner magnetometer or a three-axis 2G cryo- genic magnetometer. Weaker specimens were usually measured on a two-axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer. The specimens were demagnetized thermally in either a small Schonstedt TSD-1 demagnetizer or large furnaces described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Magnetic sus- ceptibilities were measured between heatings to monitor chemical changes. Before thermal treatment, some samples were partly demagnetized in alternating fields (AF) using a Schonstedt 2-axis GSD-5 tumbler- demagnetizer. ith euhedral quartz crystals similar to those in the overlying Mt Gee Sinter (Fig. 2e) are common. HEMATITIC BRECCIA Hematitic breccia is host to most of the uranium mineral- ization in the region. It occurs as lens-shaped bodies, up to 70 m thick, at the base and within the granitic breccia. Contacts range from subhorizontal and apparently layer-parallel, to subvertical and apparently cross-cutting (intrusive into?) the granitic breccia. With local exceptions at the metre scale, bedding is absent in the hematitic breccia. The most typical lithology consists of a chaotic mixture of partly broken and reprecipitated specularite laths, ochreous hematite, quartz and minor granitic fragments in variable proportions, plus a large number of minor minerals (Fig. 2d). These include, in order of paragenetic sequence: monazite, pyrite, chalcopyrite, molybdenite, magnetite, specular hematite, clear quartz, uraninite, later Cu-Fe-Pb-Zn-sulphide minerals including chalcocite and bornite, followed by carbonate, chlorite, fluorite and later cloudy quartz. DIAMICTITE Diamictite occurs in small outcrops and drillhole intersections along a distinct east-west trend (Fig. 1). In sharp contrast to the enclosing granitic breccia, the diamictite contains a variety of well-rounded clasts, including porphyritic volcanic and other rocks that do not occur in the local basement (Fig. 2c). The cobbles are supported by a silty to sandy matrix which is undeformed and unrecrystallized. The matrix is generally red or brown, except for parts of outcrop 9 (Fig. 1) where green portions have been partly overprinted(?) along sharp redox fronts by red material. Where exposed in three dimensions, the diamictite bodies show sharp and steep contacts with the granitic breccia, but no contact relations to hematitic breccia or quartz-hematite sinter were observed. The diamictite has been interpreted variably as stratigraphic intercalations of Adelaidean glaciomarine strata (on the basis of their striking lithological similarity with massive Sturtian tillite adjacent to the inlier; Youles 1975,1986); as solid rafts that were introduced tectonically (Drexel & Major 1987, 1990); as pebble-breccia dykes (Drexel & Major 1987); and as soft-sediment intrusive 'dykes'(Sprigg 1989). 90 M. DISCUSSION Measurements obtained in this study hav

The poles are far removed from the Cambro-Ordovician (i.e. Delamerian) part of the Aus- tralian pole path (Klootwijk 1988; Li et al. 1990). Other poles of this study, from the fine-grained siliceous sinter, hematitic breccia and granitic breccia (intermediate component) are poorly defined. These poles are consistent with the Permo-Carboniferous path, but the 95% confidence circles intersect younger path segments as well (Fig. 10). Consistently positive inclinations of remanence suggest that the ages may be Permo-Carboniferous, because this is the only period that had a prolonged reversed polarity (the Kiaman chron). Support for a mini- mum Permo-Carboniferous age for the sinter is provided by the presence of only one component of remanence in the diamictite (besides the random component in the cobbles): if the sinter had been deposited after the Permo- Carboniferous, we would expect the diamictite to contain a younger magnetic overprint corresponding to the sinter- forming hydrothermal event. Also, no major post- Palaeozoic tectonism is known for the region other than the late medial Miocene to Pleistocene uplift of the Flinders Ranges (Callen 1977), and the pole positions found here are not consistent with these periods. Samples from the sinter were collected as blocks; and those from the other rock units as cores, the latter by means of a portable diamond drill. Sample orientations were obtained with a magnetic com- pass and, nearly always, a sun compass. The drillcores were cleaned of surface contaminants by sandblasting with fine glass grit. Strongly magnetized specimens (>200 mA/m) were measured either on a Digico spinner magnetometer or a three-axis 2G cryo- genic magnetometer. Weaker specimens were usually measured on a two-axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer. The specimens were demagnetized thermally in either a small Schonstedt TSD-1 demagnetizer or large furnaces described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Uraniferous breccia in the Mt Painter region The breccia deposits and associated uranium mineral- ization in the Mt Painter and Mt Gee areas have been described by Stillwell and Edwards (1954), Youles (1975, 1984, 1986), Major (1976), Drexel (1980; 1981), Lambert et al. (1982), Drexel and Major (1987, 1990) and Higgins et al. (1988). The breccia comprises a pile of variable thickness up to at least 500 m (Drexel & Major 1987), grading from in situ fractured and K-feldspar-altered basement to dominantly granitic and hematitic breccia units (the Radium Ridge Breccias) and finally to vuggy rocks consisting dominantly of quartz-hematite-rich chemical precipitates near the top (the Mt Gee Sinter; Drexel & Major 1987; Fig. 2a). The breccia is restricted to the centre of the Mt Painter basement block and there is no evidence of stratigraphic relation to the Adelaidean sequence. It shows no metamorphic recrystallization or deformation that could suggest a Delamerian regional- metamorphic overprint. No potentially coeval volcanic rocks have been identified in the region (Drexel 1980). ith euhedral quartz crystals similar to those in the overlying Mt Gee Sinter (Fig. 2e) are common. HEMATITIC BRECCIA Hematitic breccia is host to most of the uranium mineral- ization in the region. It occurs as lens-shaped bodies, up to 70 m thick, at the base and within the granitic breccia. Contacts range from subhorizontal and apparently layer-parallel, to subvertical and apparently cross-cutting (intrusive into?) the granitic breccia. With local exceptions at the metre scale, bedding is absent in the hematitic breccia. The most typical lithology consists of a chaotic mixture of partly broken and reprecipitated specularite laths, ochreous hematite, quartz and minor granitic fragments in variable proportions, plus a large number of minor minerals (Fig. 2d). The matrix is generally red or brown, except for parts of outcrop 9 (Fig. 1) where green portions have been partly overprinted(?) along sharp redox fronts by red material. Where exposed in three dimensions, the diamictite bodies show sharp and steep contacts with the granitic breccia, but no contact relations to hematitic breccia or quartz-hematite sinter were observed. The diamictite has been interpreted variably as stratigraphic intercalations of Adelaidean glaciomarine strata (on the basis of their striking lithological similarity with massive Sturtian tillite adjacent to the inlier; Youles 1975,1986); as solid rafts that were introduced tectonically (Drexel & Major 1987, 1990); as pebble-breccia dykes (Drexel & Major 1987); and as soft-sediment intrusive 'dykes'(Sprigg 1989). 90 M. Samples from the sinter were collected as blocks; and those from the other rock units as cores, the latter by means of a portable diamond drill. Sample orientations were obtained with a magnetic com- pass and, nearly always, a sun compass. The drillcores were cleaned of surface contaminants by sandblasting with fine glass grit. Strongly magnetized specimens (>200 mA/m) were measured either on a Digico spinner magnetometer or a three-axis 2G cryo- genic magnetometer. Weaker specimens were usually measured on a two-axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer. The specimens were demagnetized thermally in either a small Schonstedt TSD-1 demagnetizer or large furnaces described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Magnetic sus- ceptibilities were measured between heatings to monitor chemical changes. Before thermal treatment, some samples were partly demagnetized in alternating fields (AF) using a Schonstedt 2-axis GSD-5 tumbler- demagnetizer. Uraniferous breccia in the Mt Painter region The breccia deposits and associated uranium mineral- ization in the Mt Painter and Mt Gee areas have been described by Stillwell and Edwards (1954), Youles (1975, 1984, 1986), Major (1976), Drexel (1980; 1981), Lambert et al. (1982), Drexel and Major (1987, 1990) and Higgins et al. (1988). The breccia comprises a pile of variable thickness up to at least 500 m (Drexel & Major 1987), grading from in situ fractured and K-feldspar-altered basement to dominantly granitic and hematitic breccia units (the Radium Ridge Breccias) and finally to vuggy rocks consisting dominantly of quartz-hematite-rich chemical precipitates near the top (the Mt Gee Sinter; Drexel & Major 1987; Fig. 2a). The breccia is restricted to the centre of the Mt Painter basement block and there is no evidence of stratigraphic relation to the Adelaidean sequence. It shows no metamorphic recrystallization or deformation that could suggest a Delamerian regional- metamorphic overprint. No potentially coeval volcanic rocks have been identified in the region (Drexel 1980). GRANITIC BRECCIA Granitic breccia, the dominant breccia type, comprises mainly clasts of local basement granite, gneiss and schist, ranging from house-sized blocks to silt-sized fragments. Sorting

ith euhedral quartz crystals similar to those in the overlying Mt Gee Sinter (Fig. 2e) are common. HEMATITIC BRECCIA Hematitic breccia is host to most of the uranium mineral- ization in the region. It occurs as lens-shaped bodies, up to 70 m thick, at the base and within the granitic breccia. Contacts range from subhorizontal and apparently layer-parallel, to subvertical and apparently cross-cutting (intrusive into?) the granitic breccia. With local exceptions at the metre scale, bedding is absent in the hematitic breccia. The most typical lithology consists of a chaotic mixture of partly broken and reprecipitated specularite laths, ochreous hematite, quartz and minor granitic fragments in variable proportions, plus a large number of minor minerals (Fig. 2d). These include, in order of paragenetic sequence: monazite, pyrite, chalcopyrite, molybdenite, magnetite, specular hematite, clear quartz, uraninite, later Cu-Fe-Pb-Zn-sulphide minerals including chalcocite and bornite, followed by carbonate, chlorite, fluorite and later cloudy quartz. In sharp contrast to the enclosing granitic breccia, the diamictite contains a variety of well-rounded clasts, including porphyritic volcanic and other rocks that do not occur in the local basement (Fig. 2c). The cobbles are supported by a silty to sandy matrix which is undeformed and unrecrystallized. The matrix is generally red or brown, except for parts of outcrop 9 (Fig. 1) where green portions have been partly overprinted(?) along sharp redox fronts by red material. Where exposed in three dimensions, the diamictite bodies show sharp and steep contacts with the granitic breccia, but no contact relations to hematitic breccia or quartz-hematite sinter were observed. The diamictite has been interpreted variably as stratigraphic intercalations of Adelaidean glaciomarine strata (on the basis of their striking lithological similarity with massive Sturtian tillite adjacent to the inlier; Youles 1975,1986); as solid rafts that were introduced tectonically (Drexel & Major 1987, 1990); as pebble-breccia dykes (Drexel & Major 1987); and as soft-sediment intrusive 'dykes'(Sprigg 1989). 90 M. The sinter (Fig. 1) consists of a mixture of three main rock types: massive or vuggy hydrothermal quartz with abun- dant metre-sized crystal-lined cavities; layers consisting of white hydrothermal quartz that apparently supports centimetre-sized clasts of coarse specular hematite, with distinct 'graded bedding' in places (quartz-specularite sinter; Fig. 2b); and finely laminated reddish-brown chemical sedimentary strata of silt-sized quartz with minor fine-grained hematite and submicroscopic, presumably hematitic, pigment (here referred to as fine-grained siliceous sinter; Fig. 2a). The overall dip of the Mt Gee Sinter is shallow, but steep dips occur locally near irregular metre scale dome-and-basin structures, which are marked mainly by the laminated fine siliceous sinter. This deformation must have occurred while the laminated material, now extremely hard and chert-like, was still plastic (Drexel & Major 1987) and is probably related to local adjustment due to differential compaction of the underlying vuggy sinter. Both the Iapetus Ocean and Tornquist Sea therefore, which separated southern Britain from Laurentia and Baltica respectively in Ordovician times, were closed by Wenlock time. As Ordovician and Silurian palaeomagnetic data from Baltica and Eastern Avalonia now record a comparable northwards translation from high southerly to near-equatorial latitudes during this time, we postulate pre-Wenlock collision of these blocks to form BALONIA (Baltica + eastern Avalonia). A new apparent polar wander path for eastern Avalonia constructed on the basis of this palaeogeo- graphic model is presented. tica and northern Britain (10-20"s). Both the Iapetus Ocean and Tornquist Sea therefore, which separated southern Britain from Laurentia and Baltica respectively in Ordovician times, were closed by Wenlock time. As Ordovician and Silurian palaeomagnetic data from Baltica and Eastern Avalonia now record a comparable northwards translation from high southerly to near-equatorial latitudes during this time, we postulate pre-Wenlock collision of these blocks to form BALONIA (Baltica + eastern Avalonia).
